figures.caption: Figure 1 | Performance on different neurons. From left to right, columns show: (1) voltage traces generated by our model; (2) voltage traces generated by PDE simulations; (3) spike-triggered voltage averages from our model, PDE simulations, and experimental recordings; and (4) F-I curves from our model, PDE simulations, and experimental recordings. For columns (3) and (4), the solid line represents the median, and the shaded area represents the interquartile range of the responses.

Figure 2 | Flow matching transforms noise to data. Columns show: (1) a draw 𝑋0 from the pointwise Gaussian noise source; (2) and (3) intermediate states 𝑋𝑡 at selected flow times 𝑡; and (4) the generated trace 𝑋1.

Table 1 | Performance by dynamical regime. Wasserstein-2 distances between reference and generated feature distributions, averaged across amplitudes in different regime types. These regimes are: (1) threshold amplitudes, where at least one HoF model produces a steady state response and at least one HoF model produces a firing response, (2) low-firing amplitudes, which produce mean spike counts between 5 and 17, and (3) high-firing amplitudes, which produce mean spike counts between 18 and 37.

Figure 4 | Spike-timing variability. Spike peak timing at representative PVALB and VIP current amplitudes, comparing smoothed spike-time densities from PDE simulations (blue), Generative (green), and NOBLE (red) voltage responses.

Figure 5 | Multimodal spike counts near depolarization block. Spike count versus input current amplitude for VIP neuron. Lines plot the mean spike count in the conditional voltage responses. Histograms plot the spike count distribution for the PDE (blue), Generative (green), and NOBLE (red) responses at current amplitudes 0.1nA, 0.18nA, and 0.28nA.

Table 2 | Performance by dynamical regime when trained on time-varying stimuli. Wasserstein-2 distances between reference and generated feature distributions, averaged across square pulse currents in different regime types. †High-firing amplitude range is cut off at 0.18nA to match the max amplitude in the time-varying stimuli dataset.

Figure 6 | Generalization to unseen time-varying stimuli. Predicted PVALB responses to unseen time-varying stimuli, comparing PDE simulations with generative models trained on time-varying and DC-step currents.

Figure A.1 | U-Net model for predicting the flow matching velocity from the interpolated voltage state 𝑋𝑡, flow time 𝑡, and input current 𝐼. Resolution is halved at each encoder stage and restored by interpolation in the decoder; skip connections carry full-resolution features around the bottleneck. Flow time and current conditioning enter every residual block.

Table A.2 | Wasserstein-2 distances between reference and generated feature distributions, averaged over amplitudes, for U-Net models trained with L1 and L2 losses. The final column is the RMS of the high-frequency residual in non-spiking traces averaged over subthreshold amplitudes, for which the reference value is 0.003 mV (closer to this is better).
Figure A.2 | Wasserstein-2 distance between reference and generated feature distributions, as a function of solver and NFE. Both axes are log-scaled.

Figure A.4 | Examples of sets of reference and generated traces for square pulse input currents to the PVALB neuron at different amplitudes. From left to right, columns show voltage traces given by (1) PDE simulations, (2) our model, and (3) NOBLE.
Figure A.5 | Variance ratio (log2 Var(Generated)/Var(PDE)) and normalized mean bias Δ𝜇/𝜎 for PVALB feature distributions at selected amplitudes.

Figure A.6 | Wasserstein-2 distances between the reference and generated inv_ISI_values distributions for sine wave inputs of varying frequencies. Voltage responses are generated for sine waves with amplitudes 0.06nA, equilibrium position 0.05nA, and frequencies from 2 Hz to 500 Hz. Smoothed Wasserstein-2 distances are plotted for the DC-step-trained model (green) and the time-varyingtrained model (orange).

Figure A.7 | Additional examples of sets of reference and generated traces for unseen time-varying protocols. From left to right, columns show: (1) the input current trace, (2) the voltage traces generated by PDE simulations, (3) the voltage traces generated by our model when trained on timevarying current inputs, and (4) the voltage traces generated by our model when trained on DC step inputs.

Figure A.8 | Examples of sets of reference and generated traces for square pulse input currents to the VIP neuron at different amplitudes. From left to right, columns show voltage traces given by (1) PDE simulations, (2) our model, and (3) NOBLE.

Table A.4 | Performance by dynamical regime, VIP neuron. Wasserstein-2 distances between reference and generated feature distributions, averaged across amplitudes in different regime types. Inv ISI is omitted in the threshold regime, where firing responses contain too few spikes to yield interspike intervals.
Figure A.10 | Variance ratio (log2 Var(Generated)/Var(PDE)) and normalized mean bias Δ𝜇/𝜎 for VIP feature distributions at selected amplitudes.
